youtube.description: In this episode you will use nullptr for a pointer that points nowhere, check a pointer before you use it and spot a dangling pointer, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 nullptr and dangling pointers · 1:17 Check before you follow · 2:18 Null and dangling · 3:07 Second program · 4:32 Recap · 5:02 Bug of the Day · 5:59 Challenge · 6:26 Next episode

scenes.narration: Today we learn about two dangerous pointers. One points nowhere. The other points at something that is gone.

scenes.onScreen: "nullptr and dangling pointers": numbered lines (1. nullptr means points to nothing; 2. Check a pointer before you follow it; 3. A dangling pointer points to a dead variable) and an analogy card: a letter sent to a house that was pulled down: the address exists, but nobody lives there
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Nullptr is a pointer that points to nothing. You can test it in an if. Never follow a null pointer. The program will crash. A dangling pointer is worse. It holds the address of a variable that no longer exists. Think of a letter sent to a house that was pulled down. The address exists, but nobody lives there. Null and dangling pointers cause many crashes. A good habit is to give a pointer a safe value at birth. If you have no address yet, use nullptr. Before you follow a pointer that may be null, test it. The test is short, and it can save the program.
points: Check a pointer before you follow it
A dangling pointer points to a dead variable

scenes.onScreen: nullcheck.cpp: a pointer is tested before it is used
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 6] P starts as nullptr. It points to nothing. [HL 7] We test it with two equals signs. The test is true. [HL 10] Now p points at fish. [HL 11] A pointer works as a test by itself. Nullptr counts as false. Any real address counts as true. [HL 12] So it is safe to follow p here. [HL 6] The pointer starts as nullptr. It points to nothing, and that is a safe state. [HL 7] This test asks, is the pointer null? Yes, so the message prints. [HL 10] Now the pointer gets a real address. [HL 11] A pointer works as a test by itself. It is true when it is not null. Then we may follow it.

scenes.onScreen: three pointers: one valid, one null, one dangling
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Here are two pointers. Good points at fish, and it is safe to follow. None holds nullptr, so it points nowhere. Never follow none. A third kind, the dangling pointer, looks like good, but its target is gone. Notice the three states of a pointer. It may point to a live variable. It may be null. Or it may dangle, and that one is the worst. A null pointer is easy to test. A dangling pointer looks normal, so it hides the bug.

scenes.onScreen: lookup.cpp: a function returns nullptr when nothing matches
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 4] This function returns a pointer. [HL 7] When it finds the target, it returns the address of that item. [HL 10] When nothing matches, it returns nullptr. [HL 16] The caller must check the result first. [HL 17] Eight is in the array, so the program prints Found eight. [HL 19] Ninety-nine is not there, so the program prints Not found. [HL 4] This function returns a pointer. It points to the item that we found, or to nothing. [HL 7] Returning the address of an array item is safe, because the array lives on in main. [HL 10] If the loop ends with no match, we return nullptr. The caller must test the result before it follows the pointer.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as lookup dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints Found eight, and then Not found. Notice that the program tests the pointer before the star. This habit prevents crashes.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Nullptr is a pointer that points to nothing. Two. Test a pointer before you follow it. Three. A dangling pointer points to something that is gone. Four. Never return the address of a local variable. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Nullptr is a pointer that points to nothing.
Test a pointer before you follow it.
A dangling pointer points to something that is gone.
Never return the address of a local variable.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Returning the address of a local
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the g++ warning appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the warning goes away with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The function returns the address of its local variable x. But x dies when the function ends. The compiler warns that the address of a local variable is returned. The pointer now dangles. Return the value instead. Local variables live on the stack, and they die when the function ends. The address of a dead variable is a trap. The pointer looks fine, but the box now belongs to someone else. Return the value, or use memory that lives longer.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the pointer see a therapist? It had too many unresolved references.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the pointer see a therapist? It had too many unresolved references.

scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a function that takes a pointer to an int. If the pointer is null, print an error. Otherwise print the value. Hint: test the pointer in an if, and follow it only in the else branch. Write your answer in the comments.

bug.error:
Compiler output (a warning, the program still builds):

dangle.cpp: In function 'int* make_number()':
dangle.cpp:6:12: warning: address of local variable 'x' returned [-Wreturn-local-addr]
    6 |     return &x;
      |            ^~
dangle.cpp:5:9: note: declared here
    5 |     int x = 5;
bug.why: The local variable x dies when the function ends. The returned address then points to a dead box. Return the value instead.
